title: Galois Group Computation for cos(2π/5)
content: The polynomial 4X²+2X−1 is the minimal polynomial of cos(72°) = cos(2π/5). Its two roots are cos(72°) and cos(144°) = cos(4π/5). The proof establishes |Gal| = 2 via: (1) irreducibility (Eisenstein on 4X²+10X+5 at p=5), (2) both roots in ℚ(α) (ring identity β=−2α²−2α), (3) splitting field degree = 2. This is the degree-2 instance of |Gal(ℚ(cos(2π/p))/ℚ)| = (p−1)/2 for prime p.
mathContext: The polynomial $4X^2+2X-1$ arises from the 5th cyclotomic field: $\cos(2\pi/5)$ satisfies $4\alpha^2+2\alpha-1=0$ (derivable from $\alpha = (\zeta_5+\zeta_5^{-1})/2$ and $\zeta_5^2+\zeta_5+1+\zeta_5^{-1}+\zeta_5^{-2}=0$, scaled by 4). The Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\cos(2\pi/5))/\mathbb{Q}) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, generated by $\cos(2\pi/5) \mapsto \cos(4\pi/5)$.

title: Algebraic Certificates: Root Identity and Factored Form
content: Two ring identities are the algebraic core of the proof. (1) root_image_beta: if 4a²+2a−1=0, then β=−2a²−2a is also a root. Algebraic certificate: 4(−2a²−2a)²+2(−2a²−2a)−1 = (4a²+6a+1)·(4a²+2a−1). (2) factored_form: 4a²+2a−1 = 4(a−α)(a+2α²+2α) when 4α²+2α−1=0. Certificate: 4a²+2a−1−4(a−α)(a+2α²+2α) = (4α²+2α−1)(−2a+2α+1). Both proved by 'ring' alone — no field operations needed.
mathContext: The root $\beta = -2\alpha^2-2\alpha$ avoids fractions: from $4\alpha^2 = 1-2\alpha$, we get $\beta = -(1-2\alpha)/2-2\alpha$, but the cleaner form $\beta = -2\alpha^2-2\alpha$ works in any commutative ring. The factored form identity is the splitting certificate: it shows $4X^2+2X-1 = 4(X-\alpha)(X-\beta)$ over $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$.

title: Irreducibility via Eisenstein at p=5 and Invertible Shift
content: The polynomial 4X²+2X−1 is proved irreducible over ℚ via three steps: (1) The shifted polynomial q=4X²+10X+5 (via X↦X+1) satisfies Eisenstein at p=5: 5∤4 (leading), 5|10 and 5|5 (lower), 25∤5 (constant). Primitivity: gcd(4,10,5)=1 (since 5−4=1). So q is irreducible over ℤ. (2) Gauss's lemma transfers: q irreducible over ℚ. (3) Since p=q(X−1) and X↦X−1 has inverse X↦X+1, irreducibility transfers. Key: primitive polynomial with gcd(coeff_0=5, coeff_2=4)=1 proved by dvd_sub argument (5−4=1 → any common divisor divides 1 → unit).
mathContext: Eisenstein criterion: for $P = (5) \subset \mathbb{Z}$, $q = 4X^2+10X+5$: $5 \nmid 4$, $5 \mid 10$, $5 \mid 5$, $25 \nmid 5$. Primitivity via $5-4=1$: any $r$ dividing both coeff 0 (=5) and coeff 2 (=4) must divide $5-4=1$, so $r$ is a unit. Gauss's lemma: $\mathrm{IsPrimitive.Int.irreducible\_iff\_irreducible\_map\_cast}$. Composition transfer: $p = q \circ \ell$ where $\ell = X-1$; $\ell^{-1} = X+1$; $\ell \circ \ell^{-1} = X$.

title: Both Roots in ℚ(α) → Splitting Field Degree 2
content: Using rootOfSplits, a root α of p exists in the splitting field. beta_in_adjoin shows β=−2α²−2α ∈ ℚ(α) (by ring operations: β = −(2α·α)−2α, all in the subalgebra). rootSet_subset_adjoin shows every root of p is in ℚ(α): using the factored form, any root x satisfies 4(x−α)(x+2α²+2α)=0, so x=α or x=−2α²−2α=β. adjoin_root_eq_top: ℚ(α) contains all roots → ℚ(α) = SplittingField. splitting_finrank: [SF:ℚ] = [ℚ(α):ℚ] = deg(minpoly(α)) = 2.
mathContext: $\beta = -2\alpha^2-2\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$: algebraically, $\beta$ is a degree-2 polynomial in $\alpha$, so it lies in the subalgebra generated by $\alpha$. The factored form $4a^2+2a-1 = 4(a-\alpha)(a+2\alpha^2+2\alpha)$ shows the two roots are $\alpha$ and $\beta$, both in $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$. Hence $\mathbb{Q}(\alpha) = \text{SplittingField}$ and $[\text{SF}:\mathbb{Q}] = [\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] = \deg(\text{minpoly}(\alpha)) = 2$.

title: Main Theorem: |Gal(4X²+2X−1/ℚ)| = 2
content: The Galois group has exactly 2 elements. Lower bound: 2 | |Gal| from Polynomial.Gal.prime_degree_dvd_card (p is irreducible, deg p = 2 is prime). Upper bound: |Gal| | 2 from Polynomial.Gal.galActionHom_injective → |Gal| ≤ |Perm(roots)| = |roots|! = 2! = 2. Together: |Gal| = 2. Main theorem: cos72_gal_card proves this via Polynomial.Gal.card_of_separable combined with splitting_finrank.
mathContext: $|\mathrm{Gal}| = [\text{SplittingField}:\mathbb{Q}] = 2$ by $\mathrm{Polynomial.Gal.card\_of\_separable}$ and separability (irreducible over a field of characteristic 0). The two-sided bound argument: $2 \mid |\mathrm{Gal}|$ and $|\mathrm{Gal}| \mid 2!= 2$ gives $|\mathrm{Gal}| = 2$. The Galois group is $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, generated by the automorphism $\cos(72°) \mapsto \cos(144°)$.

title: Constructibility of the Regular Pentagon: |Gal|=2 vs |Gal|=3
content:
The summary comment at lines 436-462 draws the key distinction between this entry and its sibling cubic cases. The degree-2 result |Gal|=2 has a direct geometric implication via Gauss's constructibility criterion (1801): a real algebraic number α is constructible by ruler and compass if and only if [ℚ(α):ℚ] is a power of 2. Since [ℚ(cos(72°)):ℚ] = 2 = 2¹, cos(72°) is constructible, and therefore the regular pentagon (5-gon) is constructible by compass and straightedge.

In contrast, the sibling entries in this family (AngleTrisectionCos20GalOQ03 for cos(40°), AngleTrisectionCos20GalOQ01 for cos(π/7)) give |Gal|=3, meaning [ℚ(cos):ℚ]=3 is NOT a power of 2. This is Wantzel's (1837) proof of the impossibility of angle trisection: to trisect 60°, one would need cos(20°) to be constructible, but [ℚ(cos(20°)):ℚ]=3.

The general pattern: |Gal(ℚ(cos(2π/p))/ℚ)| = (p−1)/2 for prime p. This equals a power of 2 exactly when (p−1)/2 = 2^k, i.e., p = 2^{k+1}+1 is a Fermat prime. The known Fermat primes are 3, 5, 17, 257, 65537 — and the corresponding regular polygons (triangle, pentagon, 17-gon, 257-gon, 65537-gon) are constructible.
mathContext: Gauss's criterion (1801): A regular $n$-gon is constructible iff $\phi(n) = 2^k$ for some $k$. For $n=p$ prime: $\phi(p)=p-1$, so the $p$-gon is constructible iff $p-1$ is a power of 2, i.e., $p$ is a Fermat prime. The formalization gives $[\mathbb{Q}(\cos(2\pi/5)):\mathbb{Q}] = 2$, which is a power of 2. The comparison table: $p=5$: $|\text{Gal}|=2$, constructible; $p=7$: $|\text{Gal}|=3$, NOT constructible; $p=9$ (not prime, but $\cos(40°)$): $|\text{Gal}|=3$, NOT constructible.
